questions.question: Describe the materials and construction of the Zulu beehive hut, the rondavel and the Nama matjieshuis, and explain where their materials came from.
questions.expected_answer: The Zulu beehive hut is a dome: saplings are set in a circle of holes with their thin ends bent over and lashed to each other and to horizontal hoops, making a basket of arches that carries every push round the curve to the ground; the frame is covered with woven grass mats and layered thatch laid from the bottom up so water runs from layer to layer, tied down with a net of grass rope against wind, with a low door against weather and heat loss and a floor of beaten earth sealed with mud and cow dung. The rondavel of the Xhosa and the Sotho mokhoro is a cylinder with a cone: walls of posts with woven saplings plastered inside and out with daga, a mud and dung mix that sets hard, keeps out wind and insects and stores heat, or of stone or sun-dried mud brick; the roof is a cone of poles tied at the apex, thickly thatched and overhanging the wall so rain falls clear, shedding water in all directions with little face to the wind, often decorated with litema earth patterns that also protect. The Nama matjieshuis is a lashed sapling dome covered with woven rush mats that let breeze through in heat and swell shut in rain, taken down, rolled, loaded and re-erected in a day. All materials came from within a few kilometres: grass from the veld, saplings from the river, mud from the pit, dung from the cattle, stone from the hillside, rushes from the pan.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by indigenous building materials being readily available, appropriate and environmentally friendly, state their honest disadvantages, and compare them with the emergency shelter requirements.
questions.expected_answer: Readily available means within walking distance, costing only labour, with skills the community already had, so a hut was built in days by family and neighbours, where an imported shelter arriving weeks late fails. Appropriate means suited to climate and purpose: thatch is a thick layer of trapped air that insulates against sun and cold and is quiet in rain, unlike iron; thick daga walls store heat and smooth the day's swings; domes and cones shed wind and water without heavy beams; low doors keep weather out; rush mats breathe in heat and close in rain. Environmentally friendly means grass and saplings regrow, mud, dung and stone return to the earth, and there is no factory, fuel, plastic, transport or waste, where a plastic shelter is centuries of litter. Disadvantages: thatch burns easily and harbours insects and needs renewing every few years, open fires inside cause smoke, daga needs yearly recoating, and over-cutting damages the veld unless resources are managed. Against the shelter list: a lashed dome is sturdy; layered thatch and eaves are waterproof but take days; only the matjieshuis is quick to erect and transportable; thatch is not fire-safe; the low door and high roof ventilate; and the buildings last years, so the investigation asks what to take from the hut rather than to build one.

questions.question: List the ideas an emergency shelter designer can borrow from indigenous housing, covering frame, cover, floor, layout and building process.
questions.expected_answer: Frame: the bent-rod dome of saplings, bamboo, plastic conduit or thin steel rod pushed into the ground and bent over, light, strong, beamless and up in minutes, with hoops to stop it spreading, and lashed or tied joints that flex in wind and can be undone to move the shelter. Cover: overlapping layers laid from the bottom up so water runs off, as a tarpaulin can be fixed; eaves overhanging the wall so rain falls clear; a low or screened door facing away from the wind; a wall that breathes with a roof that sheds; a net or ropes tied over the cover against lifting; and locally woven reed or rush mats to line, shade, insulate and make a plastic shelter opaque, made by the displaced people themselves. Floor: beaten earth sealed with mud and dung, hard, dust-free and insulating, and a raised platform or mound so the shelter stands above runoff. Layout: shelters round a courtyard for shared sheltered space, privacy and a cooking place away from sleeping areas. Process: involve the people who will live there in building, since a camp built with local materials and hands is faster, cheaper, more acceptable and better maintained; but do not borrow thatch for the camp, since it fails the one-hour and fire requirements.
